title: Pauri 6, meaning: jewels within
hook: pilgrimage bathing is worth it only if it pleases Him; the mind holds jewels when it hears the Guru's teaching (Japji 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri six. Your line was teerath naavaa. Did you say it once with the water running? Day one hundred seventy-four.

There's an old story people tell in many cultures: a man spends his whole life traveling the world looking for treasure, and comes home poor, and then finds it buried under his own kitchen floor. And so often we go looking far away for what's close. Guru Nanak's sixth pauri says something like it, standing on the riverbank we met yesterday. The jewels, it says, are closer than the river.
screen: `TREASURE UNDER THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `LOOKING FAR FOR WHAT'S CLOSE.` → `CLOSER THAN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. If I please Him, that is my pilgrimage bath; if I don't, what good is bathing? I look at the whole creation: without His grace, what does anyone receive? And then: mat vich ratan javaahar maanik, je ik gur kee sikh sunee. In the mind there are jewels, gems and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. Mat is the mind, the understanding. Ratan, javaahar, maanik: three words for precious stones, piled up so you feel the weight. And the key is sikh, which here means a teaching, an instruction. The word Sikh itself is usually traced to the same root: a learner, one who receives the teaching. On that reading, a Sikh is someone who listens for the jewels. Notice what the pauri doesn't say. It doesn't mock anyone for bathing in a river. Guru Nanak stood at those rivers, the stories say, and people still come to them. It says the bath is only as good as the heart that steps into it, and that what really washes and enriches a person is inside, waiting to be heard. Then the refrain returns: O Guru, give me this one understanding, that there is one Giver of all beings; may I not forget Him. The jewels were never imported from somewhere else. They're what's left when one teaching is actually heard. One. Not a library. A single line, taken in, can do it.
screen: `A BATH IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE HEART.` · `MAT — THE MIND.` · `RATAN, JAVAAHAR, MAANIK.` · `SIKH — ONE WHO HEARS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `JEWELS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Look inward, as if you're opening a small box you haven't opened in a while. Look for one jewel in yourself. Not something you've achieved. Something you are. Patience that shows up when it matters. A way of making people laugh. The kind of attention you give a friend in trouble. When you find one, hold it for a moment, and ask where it came from: who taught you, what line you once heard and kept. If you pray, you can thank the Giver with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Pauri six. The bath is worth it only if it pleases Him, and the mind holds jewels, gems and rubies, when it hears even one teaching of the Guru.
Your line: jewels within. Today, tell someone about a jewel you see in them. One sentence, plainly said. Day one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the sixth pauri each morning; its line about jewels in the mind is quoted in talks on why listening to Gurbani matters.

original.script: ਮਤਿ ਵਿਚਿ ਰਤਨ ਜਵਾਹਰ ਮਾਣਿਕ ਜੇ ਇਕ ਗੁਰ ਕੀ ਸਿਖ ਸੁਣੀ
original.say: mat vich RA-tan ja-VAA-har MAA-nik, jay ik gur kee SIKH su-NEE
original.note: Gurmukhi: in the mind are jewels, gems and rubies, if one hears even one teaching of the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: be good on the inside.
what it means: the mind already holds jewels, and one teaching of the Guru, truly heard, brings them out.
what a scholar hears: sikh here is a teaching, from the same root as Sanskrit shiksha and shishya; the word Sikh means a learner.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 6

notes: Pauri 6 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
The treasure-under-the-floor story is presented as a folk tale told in many cultures, not attributed to a scripture.
Sikh / sikh (teaching) / shiksha / shishya: common etymology. Confirm.
Tone toward pilgrimage bathing: the script avoids mockery. Check.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the stock line 'it keeps being true'; the sikh/Sikh shared root is now 'usually traced to', not stated flat; howItsDone no longer claims why Sikhs weigh listening.
